A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same NP-Edit work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable matching across revisions and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original image-editing and customization experiments on GEdit-Bench, ImgEdit-Bench, and DreamBooth, together with training-objective, dataset-scale, and VLM ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds human preference results, TEDBench evaluation, and further sensitivity and regularization experiments.

M1.justification: The main architecture, two-step training unroll, and VLM-plus-DMD objective remain intact. Appendix C introduces an experimental cycle-loss variant that applies reverse edits and reconstructs the input in SigLIP feature space. This variant is evaluated as an alternative regularizer rather than incorporated into the final NP-Edit objective.

E1.justification: v2 adds TEDBench evaluation, emphasizing non-rigid and background edits, and explicit object-relocation failure examples in Figure 12. The training corpora and existing GEdit-Bench, ImgEdit-Bench, and DreamBooth coverage are retained, so this extends coverage within the existing image-editing domain.

E2.justification: The retained benchmark and SFT/Flow-GRPO comparisons preserve their baseline memberships. However, the alignment comparison adds a cycle-loss-regularized variant alongside NP-Edit and LPIPS regularization, extending the comparison in v1 Figure 9 to v2 Figures 10-11. The new human and TEDBench studies reuse previously evaluated editing baselines.

E3.justification: Appendix A adds randomized pairwise human evaluation of editing success and perceptual quality, reporting 500 responses per comparison. The stated four-step schedule changes from [1, 0.75, 0.5, 0.25] to [1, 0.90, 0.70, 0.47]. Appendix F also revises the equal-compute Flow-GRPO budget from four A100 GPUs to four nodes containing 32 GPUs, retaining 2.5 days. These are substantial protocol additions and reported-setting revisions; the PDFs do not establish that existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing objective, scale, sampling-step, and qualitative LPIPS analyses, v2 adds a controlled removal-question wording comparison (Figure 9), cycle-loss experiments and quantitative regularization comparisons (Figures 10-11), and spatial-reasoning failure cases (Figure 12). These substantially broaden the investigation of sensitivity, identity preservation, and failure conditions.

E5.justification: v2 Table 5 introduces uncertainty reporting for the human evaluation, stating that all standard errors are within four percentage points. v1 provides no corresponding evaluation uncertainty estimates. This does not establish additional training seeds or repeated model-training runs.

E6.justification: Existing main-table and ImgEdit/DreamBooth appendix values are retained, but substantial new results appear. Human preferences for NP-Edit range from 48.44% to 63.19% for editing success and 71.98% to 80.39% for perceptual quality; TEDBench reports an overall score of 6.98. Appendix C adds LPIPS and cycle-loss scores, although the cycle result is inconsistent: 5.21 in the prose versus 5.10 in Figure 11. These additions do not establish cross-version performance gains.

T1.justification: The diffusion, VLM-loss, and DMD mathematical formulations in Equations 1-5 are retained. No new theorem, proof, or substantive derivation appears. Symbolic timestep notation and reversing the residual inside an unchanged norm do not alter the mathematical reasoning.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: learning editing without paired supervision through VLM gradients and DMD, competitive few-step performance, advantages over Flow-GRPO, and benefits from scaling data and VLMs. Additional evaluations support these claims without redefining them.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit dependence on VLM capabilities and biases, identifies object relocation as a spatial-reasoning failure condition, and explains why global SigLIP features accommodate ambiguous reverse edits. It also interprets the cycle-loss preservation-versus-editing tradeoff. These refine the existing discussion of imperfect identity preservation and VLM limitations.

D1.justification: v2 specifies 32 A100-80GB GPUs, provides the revised timestep schedule, and clarifies the GPU-node count in Appendix F. It also documents generating reverse instructions with Qwen-32B and introducing cycle loss after 4K iterations. Most existing hyperparameters, dataset-construction prompts, and baseline implementation details remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds citations to Esser et al. (2024) for timestep shifting, Kawar et al.'s Imagic (2023) for human evaluation and TEDBench, and Zhou et al. (2022) for prompt sensitivity. The broader positioning against paired editing, RL post-training, and diffusion-distillation research remains unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative and section order are retained, with localized wording corrections and expanded explanations. v2 updates the publication header and affiliation wording, adds LLM-use and reproducibility statements, and relocates the substantively unchanged Societal Impact text under Ethics Statement.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn to expose the existing two-step unroll. v2 adds human-evaluation and TEDBench tables, prompt-sensitivity and regularization displays, spatial-failure examples, and a TEDBench comparison panel. The former limitation figure gains a cycle-loss column and another example, while Figure 2 replaces its background-edit example. This substantially expands the visual presentation beyond renumbering and relocation.

improvement.justification: The human study adds an independent check to v1's automated evaluation, while the new sensitivity, regularization, and failure analyses make the method's strengths and boundaries easier to assess. The revised diagram and implementation disclosures also improve clarity. These benefits outweigh localized problems, but the conflicting cycle-loss scores and unexplained relationship between revised settings and retained results limit the overall gain.
